title: Reduction of CO2 to Value-Added Products on a Cu(II)-Salen Complex Coated Graphite Electrocatalyst
abstract: This work synthesizes a four-coordinate Cu(II) complex {[Cu (L2)]; 1} of the tetradentate H2L2 ligand. The synthesized complex acted as an electrocatalyst for the CO2 conversion towards C1 and C2 products by activating the stable C O bond. The catalyst ink (complex 1+DMF+Nafion; catalyst concentration ∼2 mgcm ) was surface-coated over the graphite plate to carry out the reduction reaction in a three-electrode electrochemical system. An H-type electrolyzer was employed in 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution at neutral pH in the carbonated system. A maximum amount of 36% FE was achieved at 1.80 V vs. Ag/AgCl for 60 min of reaction. The total TON and TOF of the catalyst were calculated to be 9230 and 2.6 s , respectively. The CO2-reduced products were obtained as HCOOH>CH3COOH>CH3OH>C2H5OH, which were formed through multiple–electrons transfer (2 e to 12 e ) proton-insertion reactions. The catalytic activity of the Cu(II) complex was enhanced by the presence of the terminal -NH2 anchoring-group in the ligand backbone. The fact was confirmed by electrocatalytic CO2 conversion experiments in the presence of complex 2 {[Cu(L)]; 2} as the electrocatalyst, which did not contain the anchoring group in the salen ligand structure.

Reduction of CO2 to Value-Added Products on a Cu(II)-Salen Complex Coated Graphite Electrocatalyst Paulomi Bose,[a] Chandan Mukherjee,*[a, b] and Animes Kumar Golder[a, c]
This work synthesizes a four-coordinate Cu(II) complex {[CuII (LNH2)]; 1} of the tetradentate H2LNH2 ligand. The synthesized complex acted as an electrocatalyst for the CO2 conversion towards C1 and C2 products by activating the stable C O bond. The catalyst ink (complex 1+DMF+Nafion; catalyst concentration ∼2 mgcm 2) was surface-coated over the graphite plate to carry out the reduction reaction in a three-electrode electrochemical system. An H-type electrolyzer was employed in 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution at neutral pH in the carbonated system. A maximum amount of 36% FE was achieved at 1.80 V vs. Ag/AgCl for 60 min of reaction. The total TON and TOF of the catalyst were calculated to be 9230 and 2.6 s 1, respectively. The CO2-reduced products were obtained as HCOOH>CH3COOH>CH3OH>C2H5OH, which were formed through multiple–electrons transfer (2 e to 12 e ) proton-insertion reactions. The catalytic activity of the Cu(II) complex was enhanced by the presence of the terminal -NH2 anchoring-group in the ligand backbone. The fact was confirmed by electrocatalytic CO2 conversion experiments in the presence of complex 2 {[CuII(L)]; 2} as the electrocatalyst, which did not contain the anchoring group in the salen ligand structure.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Anthropogenic activities such as the burning of fossil fuels, industrial development, etc. increase the CO2 concentration in the atmosphere, which raises the global temperature. There is an increase in atmospheric temperature by 1–2 °C for the elevation of CO2 level by about 100 ppm in the years from 1960 to 2010.[1] This menace has compelled many scientists to look for a suitable technology to convert CO2 into valuable products.[2] In the electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ERC), various hydrocarbons such as CH4, C2H4 and C2H6, and alcohols such as CH3OH and C2H5OH are generated along with CO and H2 (Eqns. 1–4).
[3,4] CO2 is a linear molecule. The central carbon atom of CO2 contains two electron pairs which are equally shared by two O2 atoms on both sides resulting in high bond strength. Theoretically, a potential of 1.90 V vs. SHE (standard hydrogen electrode) is required for the ERC reaction.[5] Not only that, CO2 and H2 exhibit a close reduction potential theoretically. Therefore, a significant amount of supplied energy is consumed for H2 evolution which would affect the Faradic efficiency (FE) of ERC.[6]

Synthesis of C2 products (C2H4, C2H6, C2H5OH, etc.) in ERC is desirable because the industrial processes for the synthesis of these products are generally complicated and energyintensive.[7] Metal electrocatalysts such as Pt, Cu, Au, Ag, etc. have already been employed in ERC where the production of formic acid, oxalic acid, and CO was the primary reduction output.[8,9] However, the metal catalysts suffer from a poor product selectivity, low FE due to the concurrent H2 evolution reaction, easy deactivation, and limited catalyst supply for their high cost in particular.[10] Among these catalysts, Cu could catalyze ERC to hydrocarbons such as CH4 (FE 27%) and C2H4 (FE 19.9%) in CH3COOK/methanol electrolyte at 3.00 V vs. Ag/ AgCl.[11] However, the Cu metal surface has a high affinity to bind with these organic compounds which adversely affect the efficiency of ERC.[12] In ERC, the CO2 molecule is first reduced to CO(ad) which is then converted to hydrocarbons through proton insertion reactions.[13] The CuO surface displays a higher CO adsorption capacity than the metallic Cu.[14] This phenomenon has inspired many scientists to synthesize such Cu-based catalysts for the production of hydrocarbons (mediated by the reduction of CO). A porous CuNPs catalyze ERC to C2H4, which is one order magnitude higher than CH4 production in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution.

This catalyst was then implemented in ERC and resulted in a threefold higher HCOOH and CH3OH formation, in comparison with the so-called wet impregnation method for Cu NPs/CNTs synthesis.[16] Cu inverse opals, synthesized by electroreduction of Cu2O, catalyze ERC to CO and HCOOH with 45.3% FE for CO and 33.6% FE for HCOOH in 0.1 M KHCO3 media.
[17] Cu halides catalyze ERC to ethylene, mediated through the formation of CO and methylene radical, with a superior FE and selectivity in aqueous KBr solution.[18]
Salen ligand-based complexes are already studied by many researchers for their ability to catalyze various chemical reactions.[19,20] A bifunctional Co salen complex containing acidic and basic sites exhibits excellent ability to capture CO2. [21] Recently, Cu(II) and Ni(II) salen-based complexes, which are capable of ERC forming CO, CH4, C2H4, and C2H6 with FE of 25%, have been reported.[22]
In this work, we report on a new Cu(II) salen complex ([CuII (LNH2)]; complex 1) and investigate its role in the ERC. Salen was chosen as the ligand backbone of the complex because of its ability to produce a thermodynamically stable metal complex. A -NH2 anchoring group was attached in the ligand backbone to examine its ability to facilitate the electron transfer process during multielectron ERC to value-added products formation. Complex 1, at 1.80 V vs. Ag/AgCl exhibited high selectivity towards the production of C2 products (C2H5OH and CH3COOH) with a high FE. Finally, to re-establish the role of the -NH2 anchoring group, a reference Cu(II) complex ([CuIIL] complex 2) without the anchoring group was also being tested for ERC and reported.

sections.heading: 2.1. Metal complex characterization
sections.text:
In Scheme 1, the synthetic routes of complex 1 are described. At first, 1 equivalent of compound A was mixed with 6 equivalents of salicylaldehyde and resulted in salen ligand H2L N°2. [22] After that, Na2S⋅2H2O was added to the solution to reduce the -NO2 anchoring group (to -NH2) of the ligand backbone and H2L NH 2 ligand was prepared.
[23] This ligand was further mixed with an equivalent amount of CuCl2⋅2H2O in CH3CN solution, where triethylamine was added dropwise to get the desired complex 1 with 73% yield.
Salen ligand H2L and corresponding Cu(II) complex (2) were also being synthesized. Ligand H2L was being prepared by reacting orthophenylenediamine (1.08 g; 10 mmol) and salicylaldehyde (3.05 g; 25 mmol) in EtOH (10 mL) as reported earlier.[24] The reaction solution was kept in refluxing condition at 80 °C for 7 h. Finally, the precipitate was collected, washed with ethanol. The resulted ligand H2L (0.159 g; 0.5 mmol) was mixed with CuCl2⋅2H2O (0.086 g, 0.5 mmol) in the presence of Et3N (0.2 mL) in CH3CN (8 mL) to get complex 2 (Scheme 2).
In the FTIR spectrum of ligand H2L NH 2, two bands for ν(O H) stretches of the two -OH groups appeared at 3496 and 3481 cm 1 (Figure S1a; Supporting Information). The asymmetric and symmetric ν(N H) stretches for the -NH2 group were
found at 3397 and 3372 cm 1, respectively. Two ν(C=N) stretches appeared at 1628 and 1615 cm 1.[23] In the FTIR spectrum of the corresponding Cu(II) complex, ν(N H) stretches of the -NH2 anchoring-group observed at 3370 and 3332 cm 1 (Figure S1b). The aldamine C=N stretch was found at 1610 cm 1. The asymmetric ν(C=C) stretch for the phenyl systems was observed at 1575 cm 1. Electrospray ionization mass spectrum (ESI-MS) analysis in positive mode on complex 1 appeared at 393.08 amu. The peak corroborated to the composition C20H16N3O2Cu as established by isotope pattern

sections.heading: 2.2. Voltammetric analysis during ERC using complex 1and 2electrocatalyst
sections.text:
In examine the metal complexes (1 and 2) as catalyst in ERC, the electrochemical measurements were performed in a bicarbonate solution at neutral pH. Bicarbonates suppress the H2 evolution reaction, and the cationic species effect H2 release with the increasing order as Li+ >Na+>Cs+>K+.[26] On the other hand, CO2 (ad) and H2CO3 species prevail in an acidic catholyte pH which could enhance H2 evolution. Therefore, the catholyte was neutralized at pH 7.0 by continuous CO2 bubbling for about 45 mins in 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. LSV scanning was conducted under 0 to 2.10 V vs. Ag/AgCl. One control LSV scanning was performed in an inert environment keeping the other experimental condition same as that of CO2 system. No reduction peak was observed. Two reduction peaks were found to appear with CO2 system (Figure 2a). The peak observed at -Ecat= 1.14 V was for the H2 evolution reaction (HER), and the peak observed at -Ecat= 1.80 V was for ERC with an onset potential of 1.20 V at complex 1/graphite WE (Figure 2a).[27] To note, Cu porphyrin complex coated over carbon fiber also exhibited a close reduction potential ( 0.98 V vs. RHE) in 0.5 M KHCO3 media producing C2H4, CH4, and CO with FE of 54% in ERC.[28]
[CuII(LNH2)] (complex 1) showed a notable peak separation of ERC and HER, which is considered as one of the primary shortcomings of many metals and metal oxides catalyzed ERC systems.[13,29] No reduction peak was observed with the inert environment at complex 1/graphite and graphite WEs, respectively. Nevertheless, the current density was lower in the inert environment than the carbonated media. The effects of the variation of scan rates are shown in Figure 2b for complex 1/ graphite WE system with CO2 bubbling. With the increase in scan rate, the current density was also increased because of the higher analyte (CO2) influx towards the electrode.
[30] ERC is a very slow process which creates a barrier for the appearance of a distinguishable peak above 30 mVs 1.

The LSV profiles in complex 2 catalyzed ERC (complex 2/ graphite WE) in the case of both inert and CO2 environment (scan rate 30 mVs 1) are illustrated in Figure 3. Unlike complex 1, complex 2 didn’t show the reduction peaks for both ERC and HER (Figure 3). The current density observed with these control systems were for the HER, which is discussed later (Figs. 3 and 5). The current density was 15.42 mAcm 2 in CO2 saturated system against 14.17 mAcm 2 in the inert environment (N2) at 1.80 V vs. Ag/AgCl with 30 mVs 1 scan rate using complex 2. That means that the current density increased very marginally in the presence of CO2 compared to the inert environment. This trend of current density is in contrary to the complex 1/ graphite WE. A current density of 20.80 and 14.51 mAcm 2 was noted during ERC for the carbonated and inert systems at 1.80 V vs. Ag/AgCl using complex 1/graphite WE at that potential. Most of the findings, ERC peak does not appear, and the higher current density is considered as the preliminary observation of a catalyst to be active. Thus, it can be argued that complex 1 was catalytically active for ERC, while, complex 2 was not. Furthermore, ERC at various constant potentials using complex 1 and complex 2 as catalysts were continued for 1 h under the same experimental condition, and the results are outlined in the following section (Figs. 4 and 5), which supported the argument.

sections.heading: 2.3. Products formation and FE during ERC using complex 1and 2electrocatalysts and Discussion
sections.text:
The constant potential analysis was conducted at six different potentials. The potentials are referred vs. Ag/AgCl. The product formation and corresponding total FE in six different electrode potentials are depicted in table S1. At 1.10 V, no CO2-reduced products were detected. H2 was the only reduced product. Formic acid (21.20 μmol/ FE 2.14%) was detected as the sole product at 1.20 V. In addition to the production of formic acid (28.5 μmol; FE of 2%), the C2 products; acetic acid (16.70 μmol; FE 5.96%) and acetaldehyde (13.9 μmol; FE 6.20%) formed at 1.40 V. The five different CO2-reduced products; acetic acid, formic acid, methanol, ethanol and acetaldehyde were detected at -Ecat= 1.60 V. The results are summarized in Figure 4a, Figure 4b and Figure 4d. The formation of formic acid further increased at -Ecat= 1.80 V (Figure 4a). The production was of 42 μmol at 20 min of ERC which reached to 64 μmol after 60 mins, and FE was decreased from 9.6% to 4.5% at

1.80 V (4b). The acetic acid formation was 28 μmol (FE 24%) and 39 μmol (FE 11.14%) at 20 and 60 mins of ERC. The production of formic and acetic acid was notably higher than methanol, ethanol, and acetaldehyde. Nevertheless, their FE was very close irrespective to the time of reaction (Figure 4b). Methanol/ethanol/acetaldehyde production of 20/11/ 12.20 μmol was increased to 26/18/20 μmol with the progress of the reductive reaction from 20 to 60 min. The corresponding FE was 13.80/15.20/14 and 5.50/7.70/7.10% at 20 and 60 mins, respectively. Total FE of 76.50% for the formation of reduction products at 20 min of ERC decreased to 36.12% at 60 min at -Ecat= 1.80 V. The decrease was due to the escalation of H2 formation from an FE of 11.50% at 20 min to 55.50% at 60 min (Figs. 4a and 4b). The transfer of protons to the working electrode side from the counter electrode side during the entire constant-potential analysis was faster with the decrease in solution pH. So, more H2 was evolved resulting in the fall of products formation.[31] The constant potential analysis is shown in Figure 4c. At 2.00 V, the rate of CO2-reduced product formation and corresponding FE decreased. The cumulative production was 112 μmol (FE 27.92%), 167 μmol (36%), and 130 μmol (FE 28.29%) at 60 min at 1.60 V, 1.80 V and 2.00 V, respectively, for the complex 1/graphite WE (Figure 4d). The hydrogen production was 569 μmol (FE 43.57%) and 896 μmol (FE 56.5%) at 1.60 V and 1.80 V, respectively (Figure 4f). The hydrogen production remained almost same at 2.00 V as that of 1.80 V.
A reference voltammetric scan was first performed for ERC only with the support-electrode (without catalyst) and it was then compared with ERC using the catalyst coated electrode (Fig S7). In the reference experiment, no product formation was observed without catalyst along with continuous CO2 bubbling (Figure S7a). It confirms that the carbon source of the reduction products is not the electrode material itself. Further with N2 bubbling, no reduced product was noted at 1.80 V vs. Ag/ AgCl (Figure S7b ).
Therefore, it can be affirmed that the carbon source of the reduction products was neither the electrode materials nor the catalyst. To support this observation, the gas chromatogram for the formation of different ERC and proton reduction products at complex 1 WE are shown (Figs. S7c and S7d).
The carbon-based selectivity (SE) for the formation of different reduction products during ERC catalysed by complex 1 was also calculated (Eq. 5).[32]

Where i describes a carbon-containing reduced product formed during the ERC and n is the number of carbon present in that carbon-containing reduced product. SE of HCOOH formation was the highest (SE 35%) followed by acetic acid (SE 21%), ethanol (SE 19.45%), methanol (SE 14%), and acetaldehyde (SE 11%) at -Ecat= 1.80 V after 60 min of ERC. A similar trend was found both at -Ecat= 1.60 V and 2.00 V except methanol and acetaldehyde. It can be seen from Figure 4d that the variation of -Ecat has a significant effect on the product yield (formic acid:
64, acetic acid: 39, methanol: 26, acetaldehyde: 20, and ethanol: 18 μmol). Nevertheless, the change in SE with the variation of -Ecat was relative less (Figure 4e). It signifies that the catalytic activity of complex 1 on the selective formation of CO2-reduced products is not affected much with the change of -Ecat.
The post electrolysis characterization was pursued by collecting the sample from the electrode surface and thereafter, XRD analysis. The peaks were obtained in the XRD analysis was for graphite powder of electrode (002), (004), (110) and no peak was observed due to the Cu or its oxides (Fig S8a). A reference scan was also added using only graphite powder of electrode surface (Fig S8b).[33] This study confirms the absence of Cu nanoparticle formation after ERC reaction. A CV analysis was also conducted after ERC analysis which was also same as before (in Figure 2a) and confirmed the stability of the catalyst (Fig S9). Furthermore, no change in current density after fourtime use of the electrode (Figure S10) consolidated the stability. After that, the turnover number (TON) and the turnover frequency (TOF) was calculated using the formula (Eq. (6)) and (Eq. (7)):[34]

The maximum TON was obtained for CH3COOH production (2852 with TOF 0.8 s 1, Table S2) followed by C2H5OH (TON 1986 with TOF 0.6 s 1) at peak potential (Table S2). TON was found to be 1151 (TOF 0.3 s 1) for the HCOOH production and CH3OH, TON reached to 1405 (TOF 0.4 s
1). The total TON and TOF of the catalyst were calculated to be 9230 and 2.6 s 1, respectively. The larger the value of TOF of a catalyst, the more active is the catalyst.[34] Thus, complex 1 as a catalyst is capable of producing C2 products by ERC.
To understand the effect of central metal ion to the catalytic efficiency, we compared the % of selectivity and product yields of complex 1 with its previously reported Ni(II) congener. While, the Ni(II) complex was more selective to EtOH [% SE/yield(μmol); 52/71] formation, Cu(II) complex (1) converted CO2 to CH3COOH (21/39) and HCOOH (35/64) under the same ERC conditions (Ecat= 1.80 V; pH=7.0, 60 min). Thus, the C C coupling and faster electron transfer rate in the case of Ni (II) complex compared to complex 1 was realized.
To investigate the role of the anchoring -NH2 group, present in the ligand backbone of [CuII(LNH2)] complex (1), towards the betterment of the catalytic performance, parent salen ligand (H2L) without the anchoring-group and it’s corresponding [CuII(L)] complex (2) were synthesized as per the previously reported procedures.[24] No CO2-reduced products were identified during the chronoamperometry analysis in the potential range of 1.60 to 2.00 V vs. Ag/AgCl in the carbonated system using complex 2/graphite WE and only H2 gas was evolved during this process (Figure 5a). The constant potential analysis using complex 2 is given in Figure 5b. H2 production was 603 μmol (FE 53.87%) at 60 min of HER at 1.80 V for the carbonated system with CO2 saturated environ-

ment at complex 2/graphite WE (Figure 5). H2 production was 291 and 834 μmol at 1.60 V and 2.00 V vs. Ag/AgCl, respectively, under the same experimental conditions (Figure 5a). Thus, this analysis confirmed that the anchoring group (-NH2 group) present in complex 1 [Cu
II(LNH2)] plays an important role in the ERC. Herein, the attached anchoring –NH2 group facilitated in the electron transfer from the electrode to the metal ion Cu(II) by holding the catalyst tightly and firmly to the electrode in the presence of Nafion binder, which is a sulfonic acid group-containing polymer. We suggest that the protonation of the -NH2 group by the polymer creates an ammonium cation and a sulfonate anion. Thus, coulombic interactions between the catalyst-molecules and the polymer occur.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text:
This study was successful in synthesizing a new Cu(II) complex (1) from salen ligand (H2L NH 2) through a metalation reaction in the presence of Et3N. The working electrode graphite plate was modified by the metal complex for the electrocatalytic scissoring of the C O bond to convert CO2 to value-added products. The best experimental condition for ERC at complex 1/graphite WE in an H-type divided cell was identified at -Ecat= 1.80 V vs. Ag/AgCl at pH 7.0, WE area of 4 cm2 and CO2 bubbling rate of 10 mL min 1. The highest FE for HCOOH, CH3COOH, CH3OH and C2H5OH production was found to be 36%. The highest selectivity was achieved for the formation of non-alcoholic CO2-reduced products such as CH3COOH (SE 21%) and HCOOH (SE 35%). In general, Cu(II)-based catalysts are known to convert CO2 to preferably C2H4 over CH3COOH, and EtOH in ERC.[35] Alcohols are produced only in the presence of a high concentration of CO. Herein, the reported catalyst is able to produce C2 products from CO2.

The supplementary information includes the experimental methods for the synthesis of complex 1, all the electrochemical processes and the characterization of complex 1.
